Noticing what changes and what stays the same helps readers understand what a story's tellers value.","futureLessons":"The questions students raise today bridge into Investigation 2, where they keep engaging with the anchor text and text sets and look more closely at how retellings change across cultures and generations.","performanceTask":"The Performance Task, Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, asks students to compare across texts and analyze adaptations. Today's book-versus-film notes are practice for that adaptation analysis."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"tone","definition":"the narrator's or writer's attitude toward a subject, shown through word choice","tier":"support"},{"word":"retelling","definition":"a new version of an older story, told in a new way or for a new audience","tier":"support"},{"word":"perceive","definition":"to notice or understand something through your senses or your thinking","tier":"support"},{"word":"adaptation","definition":"a version of a story changed to fit a new form, such as a film made from a book","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapters 1–12; Minotaur incident (pp. 57–66); bus fight (pp. 158–167)"},{"title":"Percy Jackson & the Olympians: The Lightning Thief (2010 film), selected scenes"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students quickly recall what they remember from Chapters 1–12 and rate their confidence, so you can form responsive huddles.","activities":[{"id":"launch-recall-and-sort","title":"Recall and Sort","minutes":5,"standards":[],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn to a partner. Name one event from Chapters 1–12 of The Lightning Thief that you remember best, and say how you felt as you read it. Then rate your confidence from 1 to 4: \"I can explain what happened in a scene, how the characters feel, and the narrator's tone, and how I know.\""},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today is a Flex Day. I'll meet with small groups while others work on their own. We're going back into the story we've read so far, and then we'll look ahead to where it's taking us."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which moment from the first twelve chapters is still stuck in your mind, and why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The Minotaur chase is still stuck in my mind because Percy loses his mom right before it, and then he has to fight a monster with no warning. I felt scared and sad at the same time."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Collect the ratings with a quick show of fingers. Form groups using these ratings plus recent exit tickets, annotations, and discussion notes. Students rated 1–2 should come to you first. Students not in a huddle work on the Independent Choice Work described in each huddle. You may run the huddles in any order, or skip one if your data shows students don't need it."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Through three short teacher-led huddles, students revisit key events in Chapters 1–12, compare the book with the 2010 film, and bridge into Investigation 2 with questions about retellings.","activities":[{"id":"huddle-1-revisit-key-events","title":"Huddle 1: Revisit Two Key Events in the Book","minutes":13,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Pull students who struggled to retell events, name characters' emotions, or explain the narrator's tone in recent work. Everyone else begins Independent Choice Work. Option 1: Reread a favorite passage from Chapters 1–12 and write two sentences about how a character feels, with one quoted word or phrase as proof. Option 2: Write three questions the story has made you wonder about, such as questions about gods, monsters, or why the myths are being retold today. Sample response for Option 2: \"Why does Percy's life look so much like the old Greek myths? Are the gods in this book the same as the ones in the old stories? Why do authors keep retelling these stories?\""},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Students need a two-column graphic organizer with three rows. Rows are labeled What happened, Characters' emotions, and Narrator's tone and how I know. The left column is labeled Book and the right column is labeled Film. Students complete the left column in this huddle and the right column in Huddle 2. Today's two events are the Minotaur incident (pp. 57–66) and the bus fight (pp. 158–167). Both were studied earlier in the unit, so students can draw on prior notes. Substitute other events from Chapters 1–12 if your students need a different focus."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"Minotaur incident, pp. 57–66; bus fight, pp. 158–167"},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Reteach. Events are what happens in the story. Emotions are what the characters feel, shown through actions, thoughts, and dialogue. Tone is the narrator's attitude toward the event, shown through word choice. For example, a sarcastic or joking tone can sit next to scary events."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Let's reread one event closely and fill in the Book column. We'll collect what happened, what Percy and the others feel, and how the narrator sounds, and we'll point to words that prove it."},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread the first event (the Minotaur incident, pp. 57–66). In the left column, write what happened, the emotions the main characters feel, and the narrator's tone. Include at least one word or phrase from the text as proof."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Guided Practice."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In two sentences, what happened in this event, in order?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy and Grover try to get Percy's mom to safety and run to camp, and the Minotaur chases them. Percy loses his mom, and then he fights the Minotaur and wins."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What emotions do you see in Percy, and what words or actions show them?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy feels scared, but he also feels grief and anger about his mom. I can tell because the text shows him moving fast and fighting back even though he is afraid."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How would you describe the narrator's tone? Which words tell you?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The tone is tense but still a little joking, because Percy tells the story in his own casual voice, even during the danger. That keeps it from feeling too heavy."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Quick Check. Repeat the process alone for the second event (the bus fight, pp. 158–167). Fill in the left column for all three rows, using frames: \"In this event, ___ happens. The character feels ___ because ___. The narrator's tone is ___ because the text says ___.\""},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":[],"stem":"In the Minotaur incident, why does Percy's casual, joking narration matter for tone?","choices":[{"text":"It shows the narrator is not taking the events seriously and wants readers to laugh.","correct":false,"rationale":"The joking voice is real, but the danger and grief are still serious. Humor and fear exist together in this scene."},{"text":"It keeps the tense, scary event sounding like Percy's own voice, so the danger feels personal.","correct":true,"rationale":"Percy's informal voice blends with the frightening action, so readers feel the tension through his point of view."},{"text":"It shows that Percy is not afraid at all.","correct":false,"rationale":"Percy is clearly afraid and grieving. A joking voice can be a way of coping."},{"text":"It means the narrator is describing something that did not really happen.","correct":false,"rationale":"Tone is about attitude, not about whether events happened. The events are real in the story."}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in naming events, emotions, and tone in sentences that include text evidence.","sayAsk":"Say: Point to the word in the text that shows the feeling, then say it. Frames: \"Percy feels ___ because the text says ___.\" \"The narrator sounds ___ because he uses the words ___.\" \"First ___, then ___, finally ___.\" Model: You said \"it's scary.\" We can say: \"The tone is tense because the narrator describes the chase quickly and with short sentences.\"","watchFor":"If a student names a feeling with no proof, then ask: \"Which word or action tells you that?\" If a student mixes up emotion and tone, then say: \"Emotion is what the character feels. Tone is how the narrator sounds.\" Success looks like a feeling or tone word plus a specific quotation or detail."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding the narrator's tone","tryThis":"Offer a word bank (tense, joking, sad, urgent, sarcastic, calm) and have the student reread one sentence aloud in two different tones to hear which fits."},{"situation":"Struggling with: retelling events in order","tryThis":"Give a three-box sequence strip (first, next, last) and have the student say each box aloud before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how the narrator's tone changes between the Minotaur incident and the bus fight, using one piece of evidence from each."}]}]},{"id":"huddle-2-book-vs-film","title":"Huddle 2: Compare the Book and the 2010 Film","minutes":13,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Pull students who need support comparing a text with a film version, or who skipped details in their notes. Others continue Independent Choice Work. Option 1: Choose one scene from your own notes and write two sentences about a detail you imagined while reading that a film could not easily show. Option 2: Write two sentences predicting how you think the film might show Percy's feelings differently from the book."},{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief (2010 film), selected scenes","pages":"Minotaur incident and bus fight"},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Reteach. A film adaptation turns words into pictures, sounds, and music. When you read, you build the scene in your mind from the author's words. When you watch, the filmmakers decide what you see and hear. Books can show a character's thoughts directly, while films often rely on faces, actions, and music."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Now watch the same two events in the 2010 film. Fill in the right column using the same three rows: what happened, the emotions, and the tone. Notice what you see and hear, not just what is in the plot."},{"type":"directions","text":"Watch the film version of the Minotaur incident, then the bus fight. In the right column, record what happened, the characters' emotions, and the tone, and how you know. Then, below the organizer, write notes contrasting what you \"see\" and \"hear\" when reading with what you perceive when you listen and watch."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep clips short and watch them with sound on. Pause after each clip so students can write. If the film is unavailable, play a brief trailer clip or have students recall scenes from the earlier film comparisons and note what they remember."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Guided Practice."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What happened in the film that matches the book, and what changed?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The Minotaur still chases Percy and he still defeats it, but the film made the action bigger and faster. Some details from the book are missing or changed."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How did the music, the camera, or the actors show emotions or tone?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The music got loud and fast during the chase, and the actors' faces showed fear. In the book I knew Percy was scared from his thoughts, but in the film I had to see it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did you see and hear when reading that you perceived differently when you watched?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"When I read, I pictured the Minotaur my own way and I heard Percy's sarcastic voice in my head. In the film, the Minotaur looked one set way and the music told me how to feel."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Quick Check. Below your organizer, write two or three sentences using this frame: \"When I read, I see and hear ___. When I watch, I perceive ___. The biggest difference is ___ because ___.\""},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students compare two forms of the same story using precise comparison language.","sayAsk":"Say: Use a comparison word each time. Frames: \"In the book, ___. In the film, ___.\" \"Both the book and the film show ___.\" \"The film changes ___ by using ___.\" Model: You said \"the movie is different.\" We can say: \"The film shows Percy's fear through music and facial expressions, while the book shows it through his thoughts.\" Let students whisper-rehearse with a partner before writing.","watchFor":"If a student only lists plot differences, then ask: \"What did you see or hear that made you feel something?\" If a student writes opinions like \"the book is better\" with no reason, then ask: \"What detail makes you say that?\" Success looks like a contrast that names a sense (see or hear) and a specific detail from each version."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: noticing film techniques","tryThis":"Replay a 30-second clip with the sound off, then with sound on, and ask what changed. Offer a prompt list: music, colors, faces, speed, camera."},{"situation":"Struggling with: comparing across both columns","tryThis":"Use highlighters. Highlight matching details in green and differences in yellow, then write one sentence about each color."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to explain why a director might change a detail from the book, and what that choice says about what the filmmakers think the audience wants."}]}]},{"id":"huddle-3-bridge-to-inv-2","title":"Huddle 3: Questions That Bridge to Investigation 2","minutes":14,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Pull students who are ready to look ahead, or who need support raising questions and making connections across texts. Others continue Independent Choice Work. Option 1: Write one question that emerged from a myth or story we read in Investigation 1. Option 2: Write one sentence explaining how a retelling you know (a movie, a game, a family story) is different from the original."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Reteach. In Investigation 1 you met the Perseus myth, a Raven story, the Popol Vuh, and Riordan's retelling of many myths in The Lightning Thief. Good readers raise questions while they read. Strong questions can be answered with evidence from texts and push us to think about why stories change when people retell them."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"You have been a reader, a film watcher, and a comparer. Now let's turn what you noticed into questions that will guide us into Investigation 2."},{"type":"directions","text":"Look back at your organizer and your notes on Chapters 1–12. Write two questions that emerged from the texts you have read. Then answer this one in a few sentences: Based on what you've read so far, how do you feel retellings change across cultures and generations?"},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Guided Practice."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What questions emerged from the texts you've read so far?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I wonder why Riordan made Medusa seem less like a villain than in the old Perseus story. I also wonder if other cultures have stories about heroes who find out they are part god or spirit."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What stays the same when a story is retold, and what changes?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The big patterns stay, like heroes facing monsters and testing themselves. The setting, the characters' voices, and sometimes who is the villain change."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Based on what you've read so far, how do you feel retellings change across cultures and generations?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think retellings change to fit what people care about now. Percy is a kid who struggles at school and worries about his mom, so the old hero story feels more modern and personal."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Quick Check. Write a three-sentence response: \"One question I still have is ___. I think retellings change across cultures and generations because ___. Evidence from our reading is ___.\""},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in asking open questions and sharing opinions with reasons about retellings.","sayAsk":"Say: Start your question with Why, How, or What if. Frames: \"I wonder why ___.\" \"I think retellings change because ___.\" \"For example, in ___, ___.\" \"This is similar to / different from ___.\" Model: You said \"why the story different?\" We can say: \"Why is Medusa shown differently in Riordan's retelling than in the Perseus myth?\"","watchFor":"If a student writes a yes/no or factual question, then say: \"Can you change it to start with Why or How?\" If a student gives an opinion with no example, then ask: \"What did you read that makes you think that?\" Success looks like an open question and an opinion supported by one example from a text."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: generating questions","tryThis":"Offer question starters (Why did the author change ___? What would happen if ___? How is ___ like ___?) and have the student choose one and complete it orally first."},{"situation":"Struggling with: explaining how retellings change","tryThis":"Give a two-column strip labeled Same and Different. Have the student fill in one example from the Perseus myth and Riordan's Chapter 11 before writing the sentence."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to choose one question and name a text, myth, or film from another culture that could help answer it, and explain why."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on what they noticed about the story and its retellings, and share a question they will carry into Investigation 2.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: What I Noticed","minutes":5,"standards":[],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Finish this sentence in two or three sentences: \"Reading and watching the same event made me notice ___. A question I want to explore next is ___.\" Be ready to share with the class."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did you notice by comparing the book and the film, and what question will you carry into Investigation 2?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Comparing the book and the film made me notice that the book let me hear Percy's thoughts, while the film had to show his feelings with music and faces. A question I want to explore next is why stories change when different people retell them."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Invite two or three students to share. Collect the questions on chart paper to revisit when Investigation 2 begins. Ask students to re-rate their Launch confidence as quick formative data."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"In this Flex Day, students used three small-group huddles to revisit two key events from Chapters 1–12 of The Lightning Thief, compare them with the 2010 film in a two-column organizer, and contrast what they see and hear when reading versus watching. They then raised questions about how retellings change across cultures and generations to bridge into Investigation 2.","keyActivities":["Launch recall and confidence sort","Huddle 1: Book notes on two key events (events, emotions, tone with evidence)","Huddle 2: Film notes in the right column and see/hear contrast","Huddle 3: Bridging questions on retellings across cultures and generations","Look Back quick write"],"vocabularyTaught":["tone","retelling","perceive","adaptation"],"standardsCovered":[]}}
